title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: The Battle of Borodino, followed by the occupation of Moscow and the flight of the French without further major engagements, is one of the most instructive events in history.

All historians agree that the external activity of nations in their conflicts with one another is expressed through wars, and that military success or failure directly causes the political strength of states to rise or fall.

Strange as it may seem that a king or emperor quarrels with another, assembles an army, fights the enemy's forces, wins by killing three, five, or ten thousand men, and thereby subjugates a kingdom of several millions—all the facts of history confirm that greater or lesser military success is the cause, or at least an essential indicator, of a nation's growing or declining strength. Even though it's hard to understand why the defeat of an army—a hundredth part of a nation—should force the entire nation to submit. An army wins a victory, and at once the rights of the conquering nation increase at the expense of the defeated. An army suffers a defeat, and the people immediately lose rights in proportion to the severity of the loss. If the army is completely destroyed, the nation is fully subjugated.

According to history, this has been true since the most ancient times, right up to the present day. All of Napoleon's wars confirm this rule. As Austria's army was defeated, Austria lost its rights, and France's rights and power grew. The French victories at Jena and Auerstadt destroyed the independent existence of Prussia.

But then, in 1812, the French win a victory near Moscow. Moscow is taken, and after that—with no further battles—it isn't Russia that ceases to exist, but the French army of six hundred thousand, and then Napoleonic France itself. To bend the facts to fit the rules of history and say that the battlefield at Borodino remained in Russian hands, or that subsequent battles destroyed Napoleon's army, is simply impossible.

After the French victory at Borodino, there was no major engagement—nor any truly serious fighting—yet the French army ceased to exist. What does this mean? If it were an example from Chinese history, we might call it 'not a historical phenomenon' (which is the historians' usual dodge when something doesn't fit their theories). If the matter involved only a brief skirmish with small numbers, we might treat it as an exception. But this happened before our fathers' eyes. For them it was a matter of national survival. And it took place in the greatest of all known wars.

The 1812 campaign, from the Battle of Borodino to the expulsion of the French, proved that winning a battle doesn't necessarily lead to a conquest, and isn't even a reliable indicator of one. It proved that the force deciding the fate of nations lies not in conquerors, nor even in armies and battles, but in something else.

French historians, describing the state of the French army before it left Moscow, assert that everything was in order in the Grand Army except the cavalry, the artillery, and the transport—there was no forage for the horses or cattle. That was a misfortune no one could fix, since the peasants of the surrounding districts burned their hay rather than let the French have it.

The victory that was won brought none of the usual results, because the peasants Karp and Vlas—who after the French evacuated Moscow drove their carts in to loot the city, and who personally displayed no heroic feelings whatsoever—along with the innumerable multitude of similar peasants, did not bring their hay to Moscow for the high prices offered them. They burned it instead.

Let's imagine two men fighting a duel with rapiers, following all the rules of fencing. The match has been going on for some time when one of them, feeling himself wounded and realizing this is no joke but a matter of life and death, throws down his rapier, grabs the first cudgel he can find, and starts swinging it. Now imagine that the combatant who so sensibly chose the simplest and best means to his end was also influenced by traditions of chivalry and, wishing to conceal what actually happened, insisted he had won his victory with the rapier according to all the rules of art. Imagine the confusion and obscurity that would result from such an account of the duel.

The fencer who demanded a contest according to the rules was the French army. His opponent, who threw away the rapier and grabbed the cudgel, was the Russian people. Those who try to explain the matter according to the rules of fencing are the historians who have described the event.

After the burning of Smolensk, a war began that followed no previous traditions. The burning of towns and villages, the retreats after battles, the blow struck at Borodino and the renewed retreat, the burning of Moscow, the hunting of marauders, the seizure of supply trains, and guerrilla warfare—all were departures from the rules.

Napoleon felt this. From the time he assumed the correct fencing stance in Moscow and, instead of his opponent's rapier, saw a cudgel raised above his head, he never stopped complaining to Kutuzov and to Emperor Alexander that the war was being fought contrary to all the rules—as if there were rules for killing people. Despite French complaints about unfair play, despite the fact that some highly placed Russians felt embarrassed about fighting with a cudgel and wanted to assume elegant fencing positions and deliver artful thrusts—the cudgel of the people's war was raised with all its threatening, majestic strength and, without consulting anyone's preferences or rules, it rose and fell with brutal simplicity, over and over, hammering the French until the entire invasion had perished.

And it is well for a people who do not—as the French did in 1813—bow according to all the rules of art, gracefully present the hilt of their rapier, and politely hand it to their magnanimous conqueror. It is well for a people who, at the moment of trial, without asking what rules others have followed in similar cases, simply pick up the first cudgel at hand and swing it until the feelings of outrage and revenge in their souls give way to contempt and compassion.
